query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs), toughness retention versus loss is controlled by the competition between a deformation‐induced formation of nanoscale amorphous bridges at crack tips and the tendency for atomic species to segregate at grain boundaries. When deformation conditions (e.g., low to moderate temperature and high strain rate) favor a high dislocation density with limited diffusion, local amorphization occurs at crack tips and forms energy‐dissipating nanobridges that retard crack propagation, retaining high toughness. In contrast, at higher temperatures or with slower strain rates that allow significant atomic mobility, fast nanosegregation of principal elements (such as Ni and Cr) at grain boundaries reduces intergranular cohesion and leads to premature crack initiation, thereby reducing toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, fine‐grained HEA (e.g., a CrMnFeCoNi‐type alloy) processed via standard solution treatment.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled variations in deformation conditions and post‐processing thermal treatments—specifically, adjust the strain rate and temperature during tensile or fracture testing and modify the cooling rate (or aging parameters) to promote versus suppress grain boundary segregation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted over a range from cryogenic/room temperature up to intermediate temperatures (e.g., 25°C to 600°C) at varying strain rates typical for structural applications; microstructures remaining single-phase and possessing similar grain sizes.
generation.structural_mediator: Crack tips and grain boundaries. The formation (or lack) of nanoscale amorphous regions (nanobridges) at crack tips mediates energy dissipation, while grain boundary chemistry (i.e., segregation of embrittling elements) governs the local resistance to intergranular crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures or high strain rates, limited atomic diffusion during deformation yields high dislocation densities that locally disrupt the crystalline order at crack tips, forming nanoscale amorphous regions (nanobridges) that shield the crack and dissipate energy. In contrast, at higher temperatures or low strain rates, enhanced atomic mobility promotes nanosegregation of principal elements at grain boundaries, undermining their cohesion and facilitating intergranular crack initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens deformed under conditions favoring amorphous nanobridge formation (e.g., lower temperatures/high strain rates and rapid cooling) will display higher measured fracture toughness and ductile fracture features (with evidence of amorphous bridging) compared to a baseline state. Conversely, those subjected to conditions that promote grain boundary segregation (e.g., higher temperature/slow strain rates and slower cooling or aging treatments) will exhibit lower toughness, intergranular cracking, and fewer or no amorphous bridges.
generation.baseline: Standard solution-treated HEA specimens tested at room temperature under moderate strain rate with conventional cooling (yielding a balanced microstructure without pronounced grain boundary segregation)
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply to single-phase or near single-phase, fine-grained HEAs (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi-type alloys) within the temperature and strain-rate regimes where diffusion and dislocation-mediated deformation are both active. It may not hold in alloys with significant secondary phases or under deformation conditions that fall far outside the practical range for structural applications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold conditions (temperature, strain rate, cooling rate) that shift the balance between amorphous nanobridge formation and grain boundary segregation are not precisely defined and may vary with alloy composition. Moreover, quantification of the individual contributions of each mechanism to overall toughness retention remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identically processed HEA specimens (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) and subject them to tensile/fracture testing under two controlled groups: (a) rapid deformation conditions (lower temperatures and/or high strain rates with rapid cooling) designed to minimize grain boundary segregation and favor amorphous nanobridge formation, and (b) conditions (higher temperature/low strain rate with slower cooling or predetermined aging) expected to promote nanosegregation at grain boundaries. Use in situ high-resolution imaging (e.g., TEM) during or after deformation to detect the formation of amorphous bridges at crack tips and assess grain boundary chemistry via atom probe tomography or EDS.
measurements: Fracture toughness (e.g., KJIc) from standardized tests
Fracture surface morphology via SEM/TEM to identify intergranular (segregation-driven) versus transgranular (bridging-related) crack paths
Direct imaging of crack-tip regions to quantify nanoscale amorphous bridge formation
Chemical analysis of grain boundaries for evidence of segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens under conditions predicted to favor amorphous nanobridge formation do not exhibit significantly higher fracture toughness or lack evidence of nanobridge formation, or if specimens subjected to conditions promoting grain boundary segregation do not show a concomitant reduction in toughness and intergranular cracking, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement. While strength and ductility are the global mechanical properties controlled by their bulk responses, fracture toughness originates from the resistance to crack initiation and propagation that is more closely related to the local microstructure and evolution. Therefore, the near-tip mechanisms revealed in this work, including the crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation and formation of amorphous nanobridges, could be generally applicable to the toughening of other UFG HEAs. In conclusion, we have found the deformation-induced crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation in the UFG Cantor alloy. The structural evolution exhibits a sequence of formation of the crystalline, lamellar, spotted, and amorphous patterns in TEM images that arise from different proportions and organizations of the crystalline and amorphous structures. The crack-tip high stresses, high lattice and grain boundary resistances to dislocation slip, and resulting accumulation of high-density dislocations are essential to the observed solid-state amorphization, thereby dissipating energy and resisting crack propagation.
